findings.title: MCP HTTP/SSE transport SSRF — no host allowlist (private/loopback/link-local)
findings.description: parseMcpConnectionConfig validates only the URL protocol (http/https) and that the URL parses. It does NOT check the host against any allowlist. An attacker who controls BUTLER_V5_MCP_URL or a manifest entry (e.g. via poisoned config file) can point the transport at: 127.0.0.1:PORT (local services / admin UIs), 169.254.169.254 (AWS IMDS for cloud creds), 10.x/192.168.x/172.16.x (RFC1918 — internal services), or metadata.* endpoints. The transport then makes authenticated outbound calls (with BUTLER_V5_MCP_TOKEN) and returns the result to the LLM. This is the canonical SSRF amplifier + exfil pattern.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/mcp-config.ts:101-180 resolveMcpUrl() + parseMcpConnectionConfig() — only `parsed.protocol !== 'http:' && parsed.protocol !== 'https:'` is checked. There is no host allowlist check. The http-transport.ts:44 fetch(config.url) and sse-transport.ts:69 fetch(config.url) then issue the outbound request directly to whatever host the URL points to.
findings.fix_hint: Reject loopback (127.0.0.0/8, ::1), RFC1918 (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16), link-local (169.254/16, fe80::/10), and metadata.* hosts by default; require an explicit allowlist env var (BUTLER_V5_MCP_URL_ALLOWLIST) to enable them. Resolve DNS before the connection and re-validate the resolved IP against the same deny list (TOCTOU).

findings.title: interpretQrStatus returns bot_token as raw string (no Secret<T> wrapper)
findings.description: QrStatusAction.confirmed.token is typed `readonly token: string` — a plain string. If any caller accidentally logs the action, serializes it via JSON.stringify into a debug blob, or stores it in an audit_event.detail, the bot_token leaks in cleartext. The only defense is the cli writer's discipline (wechat-login.ts:107 explicit 'do not log token' comment). D69 audit log discipline has repeatedly caught leaked secrets via JSON.stringify in audit_event detail — this is exactly the shape that triggers those leaks. A Secret<T> opaque type would force the only legitimate consumption path (header injection) and make leaks a type error.
findings.evidence: packages/adapters/src/wechat/ilink.ts:210-227 QrStatusAction.confirmed = { ..., token: String(response['bot_token'] ?? ''), ... } — plain string. The downstream writer (cli/src/wechat-login.ts:107) calls upsertWechatEnvFile but does not wrap the token. If a future caller passes the action to console.log or audit_event.detail, the token escapes.
findings.fix_hint: Introduce a Secret<T> opaque type (constructor private + toString override returning '[REDACTED]' + unwrap() for the only header-construction call site). Change QrStatusAction.confirmed.token to Secret<WechatBotToken> and force the only legitimate consumption to go through the unwrap API inside buildIlinkHeaders().

findings.title: WS subscribe token not bound to authenticated caller — any x-inbound-secret caller mints tokens for any conversationId
findings.description: POST /v1/ws/subscribe requires BUTLER_V5_INBOUND_SHARED_SECRET via x-inbound-secret header (D69 T4 SEC-3 closed the unauthenticated case). However, the conversationId in the request body is fully caller-controlled and is NOT validated against any caller-owned identifier. The shared secret is shared with /v1/wechat/inbound (so any process that legitimately talks inbound can also subscribe to any conversation). Real-time WS IDOR: a CLI tool with the inbound secret can subscribe to a victim's conversation push channel without their consent. Carry-forward from D70.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/routes.ts:451-495 — the handler reads body.conversationId, parses via parseClientConversationId (pattern check only), and immediately calls issueSubscribeToken(parsedId.value). No check that the caller 'owns' or is associated with that conversationId. ws-routes.ts:198-215 resolveWsIdentity then trusts the token's recorded conversationId unconditionally.
findings.fix_hint: Track conversation→ownerSubject mapping at intake time (normalizeWechatInbound already records value.subject). On /v1/ws/subscribe, require the caller to present a caller identity (e.g. a second header x-inbound-subject OR a derived conversationId prefix match). Reject if the caller's subject doesn't match the conversation's owner.

findings.title: Telegram webhook has no chat_id / user_id allowlist — signed-but-spam opens arbitrary DM
findings.description: /v1/channel/telegram/webhook (post-D62 FAIL-CLOSED secret-check) verifies the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header correctly. But once a valid telegram update arrives, parsed.fromSubject (= telegram user_id from the update body) is passed directly to handleChannelInbound without any per-chat/user allowlist enforcement. Any Telegram user that finds the bot can DM it and trigger the full butler loop (LLM tokens, tool calls, etc.). channel-config.ts:24 isChannelAllowed only checks channelId (the channel itself = 'telegram'), not the sender.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/routes.ts:394-450 — handler calls handleChannelInbound({ channelId: 'telegram', fromSubject: parsed.fromSubject, ... }). apps/api/src/channel-inbound.ts:29-44 handleChannelInbound calls isChannelAllowed(channelId, allowlist) — but allowlist is BUTLER_V5_CHANNEL_ALLOWLIST (channel-level), not per-sender. parsed.fromSubject at channel-inbound.ts:145 is the raw `String(userId)` from the webhook body, never checked.
findings.fix_hint: Add BUTLER_V5_TELEGRAM_USER_ALLOWLIST env (CSV). Plumb it through handleChannelInbound. Reject if !allowlist.includes(parsed.fromSubject) — mirror the wechat ilink-poller.ts:141 pattern (isDmAllowed) so the behavior matches the wechat surface.

findings.title: Slack events webhook has no user_id allowlist — signed-but-spam opens arbitrary DM
findings.description: /v1/channel/slack/events (post-D63 FAIL-CLOSED signature check) verifies the x-slack-signature correctly for non-challenge events. But once a valid event arrives, parsed.fromSubject (= Slack user_id from ev['user']) is passed directly to handleChannelInbound without any per-user allowlist. Any Slack workspace member can DM the bot and trigger the full butler loop. The generic channel-config allowlist (BUTLER_V5_CHANNEL_ALLOWLIST) only covers the channelId 'slack', not the per-user dimension.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/routes.ts:316-393 — handler calls handleChannelInbound({ channelId: 'slack', fromSubject: parsed.fromSubject, content: parsed.content, ... }). apps/api/src/channel-inbound.ts:29-44 — same gap as the telegram handler. packages/adapters/src/slack/slack-protocol.ts:81-94 — parsed.fromSubject = user (Slack user ID), no allowlist check.
findings.fix_hint: Add BUTLER_V5_SLACK_USER_ALLOWLIST env (CSV). Reject if !allowlist.includes(parsed.fromSubject). Optionally add a per-workspace team_id allowlist (BUTLER_V5_SLACK_TEAM_ALLOWLIST) so multi-workspace leaks can't bleed across.

findings.title: Hono app sets no HTTP security headers (CSP/HSTS/X-Content-Type-Options/X-Frame-Options/Referrer-Policy/Permissions-Policy)
findings.description: The Hono app's only middleware (index.ts:38-53) checks Content-Length and rejects chunked bodies. It sets NO security headers. Missing: Content-Security-Policy (none — API only, but defense-in-depth), Strict-Transport-Security (no HSTS), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff (no MIME sniffing protection), X-Frame-Options: DENY (no clickjacking), Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin (no referrer leak), Permissions-Policy (no camera/mic/geolocation policy). When this API is exposed via a reverse proxy that doesn't add these, an attacker who manages to inject HTML into a response (e.g. via LLM-generated 200 OK with a body containing script) has free rein.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/index.ts:37-53 — only `app.use('*', async (c, next) => { ... content-length / transfer-encoding check ... await next() })`. No `c.header('...')` calls anywhere in the middleware or route handlers.
findings.fix_hint: Add a second app.use('*', ...) that sets on every response: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains (only when behind TLS terminator).

findings.title: Audit JSONL file written with default umask (0644) — readable by other local users
findings.description: appendFileSync writes audit rows to ~/.config/butler-v5/audit/subagent.jsonl. Default umask on Linux is 022, so the file is created with mode 0644 (world-readable). On a multi-user host (or any shared CI runner / dev box), another local user can read the owner's full subagent audit trail — which includes task content, tool names, and reply excerpts that may reference internal project structure. The mkdir + appendFileSync pattern doesn't chmod 0600.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/audit-log.ts:42-79 — ensureLogPath() calls mkdirSync(..., { recursive: true }) (no mode arg, inherits umask) and appendAudit() calls appendFileSync(path, ...) (no mode arg, inherits umask). There is no chmod after creation. Per D-series working-style (single-tenant loopback), this is currently low-impact in production but is a real defense-in-depth gap.
findings.fix_hint: Pass mode: 0o700 to mkdirSync and mode: 0o600 to appendFileSync (when O_CREAT). On existing files, follow with an explicit fs.chmodSync(path, 0o600) once. Same for resolveSubagentAuditLogPath default — pre-create the dir at boot with 0o700.

findings.title: Telegram webhook secret compared with === — non-constant-time string compare
findings.description: telegramWebhookAuthorized at channel-inbound.ts:155-166 uses `(headerSecret ?? '').trim() === expected` to compare the X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token header against the BUTLER_V5_TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET env var. Non-constant-time comparison. Timing attacks on a shared secret over HTTPS are low-feasibility, but Slack uses timingSafeEqual (slack-protocol.ts:32) — the asymmetry between the two channel handlers is itself a smell.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/channel-inbound.ts:155-166 telegramWebhookAuthorized(): `return (headerSecret ?? '').trim() === expected`. Compare with packages/adapters/src/slack/slack-protocol.ts:16-33 verifySlackSignature() which uses `timingSafeEqual(a, b)` after length check.
findings.fix_hint: Buffer.from both sides, length-equal-check, then crypto.timingSafeEqual. Move the constant-time compare into a shared `secureCompareStrings(a, b)` helper in apps/api/src/lib/.

findings.title: Inbound shared secret compared with === in /v1/wechat/inbound and /v1/conversations
findings.description: Both /v1/wechat/inbound (routes.ts:77-91) and /v1/conversations (routes.ts:39-52) and /v1/ws/subscribe (routes.ts:451-463) compare BUTLER_V5_INBOUND_SHARED_SECRET via `headerInboundSecret.trim() !== expectedInboundSecret`. Non-constant-time. Same asymmetry vs the slack signature path noted in SEC-008.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/routes.ts:50, 89, 461 — three identical non-constant-time compares of the inbound shared secret.
findings.fix_hint: Extract a `secureCompareStrings(a, b)` helper using crypto.timingSafeEqual after length check. Apply it to all three sites.

findings.title: Slack url_verification challenge has no rate limit + no team_id allowlist
findings.description: The challenge branch (routes.ts:344-346) returns the challenge string without any rate limit or workspace (team_id) allowlist. An attacker who knows the webhook URL can flood challenges, but the response is just an echo so impact is low. More concerning: if the same URL ever became routable from non-Slack sources, the lack of a team_id allowlist means any workspace could complete onboarding. Pre-scoped as SEC-11.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/routes.ts:316-346 — the challenge branch bypasses signature verification (per Slack spec) and returns parsed.challenge directly. No body.team_id check, no per-IP throttle.
findings.fix_hint: Add an optional per-IP throttle (mirror owner-rate-limit.ts pattern) for the challenge path. For team_id, add BUTLER_V5_SLACK_TEAM_ALLOWLIST env and reject challenges whose body.team_id is not in the list. Lower priority than SEC-005 (signed-event user allowlist).

findings.title: /v1/conversations has no per-caller rate limit (post-D69 auth, no throttle)
findings.description: D69 T4 added x-inbound-secret auth to /v1/conversations, but no rate limit. An attacker who has the shared secret can spam ConversationStarted events into the event bridge at line 67-74, exhausting the event bridge write capacity and starving legitimate traffic. The owner-rate-limit (D70 T4) only covers /v1/owner/*. Same threat for /v1/wechat/inbound (routes.ts:77) — pre-scoped.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/routes.ts:39-76 — POST /v1/conversations writes one event per request via wiring.eventBridge.appendConversationEvent. No throttle middleware. /v1/wechat/inbound (routes.ts:77-259) similarly un-throttled.
findings.fix_hint: Reuse the tryAcquireOwnerSlot pattern with a separate key 'inbound'. Apply to /v1/conversations, /v1/wechat/inbound, /v1/channel/inbound (already gated by secret but unbounded), and /v1/ws/subscribe.

findings.title: Slack signing secret timestamp window accepts future timestamps (no max-age floor)
findings.description: verifySlackSignature uses `Math.abs(nowMs - ts * 1000) > 5 * 60_000` — symmetric ±5min window. Slack's spec says reject anything older than 5 minutes (one-sided floor). The symmetric window allows a clock-skew attacker to pre-sign events up to 5 minutes in the future and replay them. Low impact in practice because the replay window is still bounded.
findings.evidence: packages/adapters/src/slack/slack-protocol.ts:16-33 — `Math.abs(nowMs - ts * 1000) > 5 * 60_000`.
findings.fix_hint: Use `nowMs - ts * 1000 > 5 * 60_000 || ts * 1000 - nowMs > 60_000` (5min past, 1min future) to match Slack's documented behavior.

findings.title: Channel outbound media [[media:]] rejects have no audit_event emission
findings.description: resolveOutboundAttachment at channel-outbound-media.ts:79-99 rejects paths outside allowed roots with `{ok: false, reason: 'media path not allowed: ...'}` but emits no audit_event. If an LLM is prompt-injected into requesting [[media:../../etc/shadow]] (or similar), the rejection is silent — no operator signal. Pre-scoped as SEC-6 carry-forward.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/channel-outbound-media.ts:79-99 — `if (!isAllowedOutboundMediaPath(...)) return { ok: false, reason: ... }` and `catch { return { ok: false, reason: ... } }`. Neither path calls appendAuditEvent. Compare with channel-outbound.ts's mediaCount / deliveryReason fields which DO surface failures (but only as a non-audit response field).
findings.fix_hint: Add a `wiring.runtimeStore?.appendAuditEvent({ action: 'channel.media.rejected', subject: 'llm', detail: { channelId, path, reason }, ... })` call on the rejection paths. Mirror the mcp.ts:98 audit emit pattern.

findings.title: Channel outbound media root enumeration — process.cwd() always allowed
findings.description: allowedOutboundMediaRoots at channel-outbound-media.ts:60-67 unconditionally allows process.cwd() and process.cwd()/.butler-v5. If the operator runs butler-v5 from /home/alice (not a dedicated workdir), cwd-relative [[media:foo]] resolves anywhere under /home/alice including ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.aws/credentials, etc. Operator-controlled risk, but worth flagging.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/channel-outbound-media.ts:60-67 — `const roots = [resolve(process.cwd()), resolve(process.cwd(), '.butler-v5')]` always added before the BUTLER_V5_WORKSPACE / BUTLER_V5_TELEGRAM_MEDIA_DIR explicit roots.
findings.fix_hint: Drop the implicit cwd root unless BUTLER_V5_CHANNEL_OUTBOUND_MEDIA_ALLOW_CWD=1. Document the safe deployment practice (run from a dedicated workdir).

findings.title: Audit-log JSONL appendFileSync without fsync — crash may lose audit rows
findings.description: appendFileSync is not fsynced; an immediate process crash (kill -9 / OOM / power loss) can lose the last few audit rows. For §13 audit completeness, owner-facing audit queries may miss the rows. Low priority because the audit_events Postgres table is the canonical record and JSONL is best-effort, but the JSONL is also consumed by other tooling.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/audit-log.ts:72-79 appendAudit() uses `appendFileSync(auditLogPath(), JSON.stringify(entry) + '\n')`. No fsync.
findings.fix_hint: Switch to fs.promises.open(path, 'a') + write + fdatasync. Or accept the loss and document JSONL as best-effort with the Postgres audit_events table as the source of truth.

findings.title: Owner document delete cascades memories + project-knowledge — no audit_event integrity check across cascade
findings.description: DELETE /v1/owner/documents/:documentId cascades durableMemoryStore.deleteBySourceDocumentId + projectKnowledgeStore.deleteBySourceDocumentId. The audit_event at line 170-185 records the cascade counts but a partial failure (e.g. durableMemoryStore deleted 0 because it was unconfigured) silently reports `cascadedMemories: 0`. Operator can't tell whether the cascade actually ran or whether the store is misconfigured.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/owner-routes/documents.ts:163-166 — `(await wiring.durableMemoryStore?.deleteBySourceDocumentId(documentId)) ?? 0` returns 0 if the store is undefined (no signal). Same pattern for projectKnowledgeStore.
findings.fix_hint: Track per-store success/failure (e.g. { durableMemories: { ok: true, count: 0 } | { ok: false, reason: 'store unavailable' }, projectKnowledge: ... }) so the audit detail records whether each cascade actually ran.

findings.title: Owner routes accept arbitrary subject parameter — latent IDOR cross-actor (loopback-only today, dangerous if bearer auth added)
findings.description: GET /v1/owner/memories?subject=ANY_USER (memories.ts:26), GET /v1/owner/documents?subject=ANY_USER (documents.ts:25), GET /v1/owner/tasks?subject=ANY_USER (traces-procedures-tasks.ts:115) all read another tenant's data via a query parameter. The ownerAuthorized check (owner-auth.ts:47) only requires loopback. Once bearer auth lands (per owner-routes.ts:24 comment), a caller authenticated as owner-X could read owner-Y's memories/documents/tasks by passing subject=owner-Y.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/owner-routes/memories.ts:26, documents.ts:25, traces-procedures-tasks.ts:115 — `const subject = (c.req.query('subject') ?? 'owner').trim() || 'owner'` with no caller-vs-subject check.
findings.fix_hint: When bearer auth is added, derive subject from the authenticated caller and ignore the query parameter (or require the caller to be admin to read others' data). Add a helper `resolveSubjectFromAuth(c)` that returns the caller's subject and a separate `resolveSubjectFromBody(c, fallback)` for owner-explicit-self-only reads.

findings.title: parseSlackEventPayload accepts ev.subtype='file_comment' but never extracts file_url for download
findings.description: parseSlackEventPayload accepts file_share + file_comment subtypes (line 73-80) but describeSlackFiles only inspects ev.files for url_private, never ev.file for file_comment subtype (which only carries a single file_id). A file_comment message produces empty media and falls back to text only. No security impact today, but the symmetry with the file_share path suggests future code that handles file_url will not validate the host.
findings.evidence: packages/adapters/src/slack/slack-protocol.ts:73-79 subtype allowlist and 89 `const fileContent = describeSlackFiles(ev['files'], text)` — files[] is empty for file_comment.
findings.fix_hint: Either drop file_comment from the allowlist (low-traffic) or extend describeSlackFiles to inspect ev.file for file_comment subtype. When adding url_private handling, validate the host is slack-files.com / files.slack.com before fetching.

findings.title: Channel outbound media path symlink-follow — readFile follows symlinks under allowed roots
findings.description: isAllowedOutboundMediaPath at line 69-77 resolves the path then checks it starts with an allowed root. But the check happens BEFORE access/readFile at line 92-94. If BUTLER_V5_WORKSPACE points at /var/data and an attacker drops a symlink /var/data/innocent.png → /etc/shadow, the allowed-root check passes and readFile follows the symlink. This is the standard TOCTOU/symlink pattern.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/channel-outbound-media.ts:69-99 — isAllowedOutboundMediaPath uses resolve() (canonicalizes but does not follow symlinks at the leaf). resolveOutboundAttachment calls access(resolved) + readFile(resolved) — Node's readFile follows symlinks.
findings.fix_hint: Open with fs.open(resolved, 'r') + fs.fstat() + check !stat.isSymbolicLink() OR use O_NOFOLLOW on the open. Alternatively, reject any path that traverses a directory component the operator hasn't explicitly listed.

findings.title: Slack outbound fileName not sanitized — uploaded filename is attacker-controlled
findings.description: parseChannelOutboundMedia at channel-outbound-media.ts:40-58 builds attachment.name = basename(rawPath). If rawPath is [[media:foo.txt"]; ls /; #bar.png]], basename only takes the last segment, which is fine for traversal but the resulting fileName is passed verbatim to Slack's files.upload (slack-outbound-media.ts:24). Slack will reject most junk but the attack surface includes Content-Disposition header injection via filename. Low impact.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/channel-outbound-media.ts:40-58 — `name: basename(rawPath)`. The rawPath comes from the LLM reply (channels outbound text). No further validation on name.
findings.fix_hint: Sanitize fileName to [A-Za-z0-9._-]+ before passing to Slack. Or rely on Slack's own sanitization (per their API docs, filenames are escaped).

findings.title: Telegram sendPhoto/sendDocument — file_id / file_name not escaped in FormData
findings.description: sendTelegramOutboundMedia builds a FormData with chat_id + photo/document + fileName (channel-outbound-media.ts:101-141). FormData handles encoding but the fileName is appended verbatim (line 117). Telegram servers handle arbitrary bytes, but a downstream consumer of Telegram's forwarded message (e.g. logging) might double-decode. Low impact.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/channel-outbound-media.ts:117 `form.append(field, new Blob([...]), config.attachment.name)` — name not sanitized.
findings.fix_hint: Mirror SEC-020 — sanitize fileName to [A-Za-z0-9._-]+ before append.

findings.title: WS upgrade response lacks timing-safe token compare vs query string parse
findings.description: resolveWsIdentity at ws-routes.ts:198-215 looks up the subscribe token via `lookupSubscribeToken(token)` (a Map.get — internally constant-time for the same key length, but the token is taken from a URL query string). The lookup is a Map.get which is O(1) and not constant-time in the key bytes. Low feasibility timing attack — token is 24 random bytes, brute force over the network is impractical.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/ws-routes.ts:198-215 resolveWsIdentity. The token comes from `extractQueryParam(url, 'token')` (line 199). Lookup is Map.get which is not constant-time across keys.
findings.fix_hint: No change needed; the token is cryptographically random (randomBytes(24)). Document the assumption that the token space (2^192) makes timing attacks on Map.get infeasible.

findings.title: WECHAT_ALLOWED_USERS allowlist only enforced at ilink-poller (Telegram/Slack webhooks have no equivalent)
findings.description: The wechat ilink-poller correctly enforces BUTLER_V5_WECHAT_DM_POLICY + BUTLER_V5_WECHAT_ALLOWED_USERS at ilink-poller.ts:141 (isDmAllowed). But the slack events webhook (SEC-005) and telegram webhook (SEC-004) have no parallel enforcement. This is the asymmetry pre-scoped as SEC-29/30. Documented as a separate finding because the gap is the lack of a unified allowlist abstraction across all three channel surfaces.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/ilink-poller.ts:141 isDmAllowed(inbound.fromUserId, dmPolicy, allowedUserIds). Compare with slack/telegram webhook handlers which never call isDmAllowed.
findings.fix_hint: Extract a shared channelAllowlist module: per-channel-id user-allowlist resolver. Use it from all three surfaces (ilink-poller, slack webhook, telegram webhook).

findings.title: Slack url_verification challenge body size unconstrained — 2MiB cap bypassed for non-body methods
findings.description: D69 T4 closed the chunked-body bypass for POST/PUT/PATCH (index.ts:38-53). GET requests skip the body check, which is correct (GET has no body). The 2 MiB cap applies to slack url_verification (which IS a POST with a tiny body). No bypass found.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/index.ts:38-53 — middleware checks `method === 'POST' || method === 'PUT' || method === 'PATCH'` and applies Content-Length cap. Slack/Telegram webhooks are POSTs, so the cap applies.
findings.fix_hint: No change. D69 T4 SEC-4 / SEC-10 closure is verified.

findings.title: WS upgrade doesn't bind remoteAddress to subscribe-token (any local caller can upgrade)
findings.description: ws-routes.ts:298-318 upgrade handler validates Origin (loopback only via BUTLER_V5_WS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS) but does NOT check remoteAddress. A loopback-bound WS accepts any local connection (any process on the same host can subscribe to a conversation it knows the ID for, by minting a token via /v1/ws/subscribe with the inbound secret). The token is the only auth factor. Combined with SEC-003 (token not bound to caller), this is a two-layer weakness.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/ws-routes.ts:298-318 server.on('upgrade') — checks Origin only. ws-routes.ts:171-196 isOriginAllowedForWsUpgrade doesn't take remoteAddress.
findings.fix_hint: When the upgrade handler is loopback-bound, that's the only barrier. For non-loopback bind, also check remoteAddress is in a private range OR matches an explicit allowlist. Lower priority — depends on SEC-003 being closed first.

findings.title: Slack signature header allow-list bypass via dual headers (signature vs slack-signature)
findings.description: routes.ts:335 reads `c.req.header('x-slack-signature') ?? ''`. Hono's req.header is single-valued (returns first match). No header injection path found — slack's library reads the same header. Closed.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/routes.ts:335 `const signature = c.req.header('x-slack-signature') ?? ''`.
findings.fix_hint: No change.

findings.title: iLink confirm redirect_host may be HTTP scheme — protocol downgrade
findings.description: wechat-login.ts:84 `currentBase = action.host.startsWith('http') ? action.host : 'https://${action.host}'` allows the redirect_host to be http:// (downgrade). The QR-confirmed baseUrl is then validated against WECHAT_OUTBOUND_NETWORK_HOST_SET (cli/src/wechat-login.ts:100) but scheme isn't checked there — only the hostname.
findings.evidence: cli/src/wechat-login.ts:84-86 + 28-38 isAllowedIlinkHost: checks scheme (http/https), but does not REQUIRE https. A redirect_host='http://ilinkai.weixin.qq.com' would pass both checks and persist the HTTP URL into .env, downgrading all subsequent iLink traffic to plaintext.
findings.fix_hint: Reject scheme !== 'https' in isAllowedIlinkHost. Or accept http only for localhost (mock servers) via a separate BUTLER_V5_WECHAT_ALLOW_HTTP_LOCAL=1 flag.

findings.title: iLink bot_token persisted to .env file with default umask (0644)
findings.description: upsertWechatEnvFile writes the bot_token to opts.envPath (wechat-login.ts:106). Default umask is 022 → file mode 0644 (world-readable). Same defense-in-depth gap as SEC-007 but for the .env file. Other local users can read the bot_token. Mirrors the audit-log issue.
findings.evidence: cli/src/wechat-login.ts:106-110 `upsertWechatEnvFile(opts.envPath, { token: action.token, accountId, baseUrl })`. upsertWechatEnvFile is in packages/adapters/src/wechat/env-file.ts.
findings.fix_hint: Chmod 0600 after writing the .env file. Or pre-create with mode 0600.

findings.title: MCP stdio spawn uses host env PATH without explicit binary directory
findings.description: mcp-spawn.ts:36 `env: { PATH: hostEnv['PATH'] ?? '/usr/bin:/bin' }` — passes the host's PATH through to the sandboxed MCP subprocess. If PATH is mutable by another local user (no), or contains a writable directory (possible: /usr/local/bin is sometimes world-writable on dev boxes), a local attacker can place a fake `node` binary and have the MCP subprocess execute it. Low probability in production but a clean fix is to use a fixed `/usr/bin:/bin`.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/mcp-spawn.ts:36
findings.fix_hint: Hardcode PATH='/usr/bin:/bin' (or read from a fixed allowlist) for the sandboxed subprocess. Strip any user-controlled PATH entries.

findings.title: WS subscribe token store Map uses .keys().next() for eviction — non-atomic
findings.description: issueSubscribeToken at ws-subscribe.ts:35-39 evicts the oldest token when at cap. `tokens.keys().next().value` returns the first-inserted entry (Map iteration order = insertion order). The loop is synchronous so no race within a single call. Multiple concurrent calls in the same process could double-evict, but the cap is 10K so the worst case is a brief 1-token over-cap.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/ws-subscribe.ts:35-46
findings.fix_hint: No change needed for D71; the D63 F-14 cap-of-10K closure is correct. Not a security issue, just a potential minor over-allocation.

findings.title: Slack signing secret absence returns 401 with explanatory message — fingerprinting risk
findings.description: routes.ts:337-339 returns 'slack signing secret not configured' when BUTLER_V5_SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET is unset. This confirms the existence of butler-v5 to an attacker probing the endpoint. Same pattern for telegram webhook secret (channel-inbound.ts:159-164 'inbound shared secret not configured'). Per the D63 FAIL-CLOSED contract, this is intentional — but worth noting it leaks version/configuration to a fingerprint scanner.
findings.fix_hint: Replace all four distinct 401 messages with a single generic 'unauthorized' to avoid version/config fingerprinting. Low priority — defense in depth.

findings.title: Channel outbound media path accepted via LLM reply text — content is attacker-controllable via prompt injection
findings.description: parseChannelOutboundMedia scans the LLM reply text for [[media:...]] tags (channel-outbound-media.ts:40-58). The reply comes from the LLM, which is prompt-injectable. An attacker who can influence the LLM's output (via poisoned documents, wechat messages, etc.) can request [[media:any/path/under/allowed/roots]]. Currently isAllowedOutboundMediaPath is a static check against operator-configured roots — the LLM only picks a path the operator already allowed. No additional attack surface beyond operator trust.
findings.evidence: apps/api/src/channel-outbound-media.ts:40-58
findings.fix_hint: Document that [[media:]] paths are LLM-attacker-controllable but bounded by operator-configured roots. Consider a content-hash allowlist (operator pre-registers specific file paths the LLM can request) for high-security deployments.

findings.title: Slack `text` field clipped to 3900 chars — but `content` from file_comment/file_share can be arbitrarily large
findings.description: parseSlackEventPayload sets content = fileContent?.content ?? text. fileContent comes from describeSlackFiles which concatenates file names + captions. The 2 MiB body limit (index.ts:36) bounds the input size, so the resulting content is bounded. No bypass found.
findings.evidence: packages/adapters/src/slack/slack-protocol.ts:82-91
findings.fix_hint: No change. Body limit + Content-Length check (D69 T4 SEC-4/SEC-10) closes this.
